So these notes come from the commentary text that came back in search results, not from complete pages. Several things you asked for are missing because of that. They are listed at the end.

# Psalm 41: Research notes

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Title / overview.** Guzik quotes Alexander Maclaren: the centre of the psalm shows David suffering from two things, sickness and treacherous friends. Guzik ends by saying David cares more about God's lasting favour than about his enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/
Matthew Henry outlines it this way: David holds on to God's promises while sick (vv. 1–4), then describes his enemies' malice (vv. 5–9). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_041.cfm

**v. 1**
- "Poor" means more than lacking money. It covers the weak and helpless. "Considers" (quoting Kidner) means thinking carefully about the person's situation, not giving token help. Guzik adds that much charity fails this test because it creates long-term dependence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/
- Pulpit: the word is less about actual poverty and more about humiliation and weakness. God shows pity to those who show pity (cross-references include Matthew 6:14–15 and Proverbs 19:17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/41.htm
- Spurgeon: such people find out the causes of someone's troubles and actually help, instead of tossing a coin and moving on. He also says Christ is above all the one who "considered" our low condition. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm
- Barnes: the Hebrew verb means to look at, then to act wisely. The "poor" are anyone weak through poverty, sickness or a low position. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/41-1.htm
- Maclaren: David is quietly applying these general promises to himself. He has shown mercy, and he trusts he will receive mercy, even though things look dark. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/41.htm

**v. 2**
- Pulpit and Maclaren: the Hebrew of the last line is a prayer ("do not deliver him…"), not a flat statement. The psalmist moves from teaching into prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/41.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/41.htm
- Matthew Henry: the promise is that such people will be kept alive, not that they will be promoted. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_041.cfm
- Spurgeon: if earthly gains don't come, spiritual ones will be doubled. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm

**v. 3.** Commentators disagree on what "turn/make all his bed" means. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/41-3.htm
- **Comfort while still sick:** Barnes and Gill take it as God easing the sick person, like a nurse remaking the bed, not necessarily curing him. Pulpit leans this way too.
- **Healing:** Ellicott, the Cambridge Bible, and Keil & Delitzsch read "turn" as "change": God changes sickness into health. A note quoted in Spurgeon's Treasury says the same. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm
- John Trapp allows both readings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-41.cfm
- Matthew Henry: God has not promised his people they will never be sick, or that a sickness won't end in death. He has promised to help them bear it patiently. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_041.cfm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: this is a confession with no excuses, made to God himself. David's sick soul mattered more than his sick body. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/
- Spurgeon's sermon "A Singular Plea in Prayer": strangely, the confession is the argument. David is saying, "I have sinned, so I have no claim; glorify your free grace." https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-singular-plea-in-prayer
- Pulpit: his own sin is the root of all his troubles. Matthew Henry and Benson: sin is the soul's sickness, and pardon and renewal heal it. Barnes: David saw his sin as the cause of his illness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/41-4.htm
- Trapp: heal the inside first, then the body. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/psa-41.cfm
- Guzik, quoting VanGemeren: there is no despair here; it may be a general confession of sins David wasn't aware of. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: David's enemies expected him to die soon and wanted his memory wiped out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/41.htm
- Barnes: it is hard to imagine anything crueller than wishing a sick man dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-41.html
- Guzik, quoting Boice: jealousy and lust for power explain why a good king had so many enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: the false visitor's heart works like a magnet, pulling evil in. Boice imagines courtiers saying kind words they didn't mean. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/
- Spurgeon: spite can spin webs out of nothing; the visitor makes up lies and then sells them in the open market. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm
- Maclaren: the visitor watches closely for signs of weakness, then reports them as soon as he leaves the room. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/41.htm

**v. 7.** The NET note says the verb means whispering to one another. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=41
Spurgeon asks why they whisper: are their plans too treacherous to say aloud? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/

**v. 8.** The Hebrew reads literally "thing of Belial/worthlessness".
- NET: here it probably means the illness itself. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=41
- Pulpit: more likely a shameful accusation poured over him "like molten metal". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/41.htm
- Barnes: a "sentence of destruction", meaning they think God is punishing him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-41.html

**v. 9**
- The literal Hebrew is "man of my peace". Eating someone's bread means living as part of his household, and lifting the heel is like a horse kicking a kind master (Preacher's Homiletical Commentary). Barclay: in the East, sharing bread was a pledge of loyalty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/41-9.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/13-18.html
- Clarke (on John 13:18): David originally meant Absalom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/13-18.html
- Gill mentions a writer who connects the false visitor in v. 6 with Absalom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/41.htm
- How this verse relates to Judas is debated; see Section 2.

**v. 10**
- Kidner (in Guzik): asking to repay them himself is unusual, because the psalms usually ask God to do the repaying. Guzik: as the LORD's anointed, David felt this was justified. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/
- Pulpit: this was a king's duty, not private revenge (citing Romans 13:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/41.htm
- Spurgeon: as a ruler David could rightly want offenders punished. But the line as written belongs to the Old Testament and is "quite aside from the spirit of Christianity", and Spurgeon points readers to the gospel's better spirit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm

**v. 11.** Pulpit: "favourest" can also be translated "delightest in". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/41.htm
NET: "by this" may point to a word from God promising rescue, which is assumed but not quoted (citing Craigie). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=41

**v. 12**
- Guzik: David needed God to hold him in his integrity. Being "set before Your face" (God's favour and friendship) mattered most to him, and he spoke of it as something he already had. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-41/
- Matthew Henry: no one keeps his integrity any longer than God upholds him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_041.cfm
- Spurgeon: our integrity is both comparative and dependent on God, which should humble us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm

**v. 13**
- Maclaren: this blessing is not part of the psalm itself. It was added to close the first book of Psalms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/41.htm
- NET: the double "Amen" is probably the congregation's response. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=41
- Spurgeon: "God of Israel" is God's covenant title. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm

## 2. Where Protestant teachers differ

**Is the whole psalm about Christ? (vv. 1–12)** This is a split within the Baptist tradition.
- **John Gill (Baptist):** because Jesus applies v. 9 to Judas, Gill reads the whole psalm as being about Christ. The "poor one" of v. 1 is Christ himself. The enemies of v. 5 are the Jews who wanted him dead. In v. 4 he says "I have sinned" can also be read "I have made a sin offering", so the line is about Christ's atonement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/41.htm
- **C. H. Spurgeon (Baptist):** he draws Christ out of many verses but says plainly that the "strained application" of every sentence to Christ "is not to our liking". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm

**v. 9: prophecy or pattern?**
- **Direct prophecy by the Spirit:** Wesley's Notes (Methodist/Arminian) and Benson (Methodist), following Poole: the words were literally true of David, but the Holy Ghost "looked further" to Christ and Judas. Matthew Henry: David, "in the Spirit", spoke of Judas. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/41-9.html
- **Pattern, not prediction:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (labelled Calvinist on the site) says the verse is "not distinctly prophetical". David is a type of Christ, and "that the Scripture may be fulfilled" has a broad meaning in the New Testament. Barnes says Judas belonged to the same class of person the psalm describes. Coffman (Restoration Movement) sees no justification for calling it a Messianic psalm, though he notes Leupold called it "indirectly Messianic". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/41-9.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-41.html
- **Maclaren (Baptist):** Jesus' quotation doesn't make the psalm Messianic. He points out that Jesus leaves out "in whom I trusted". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-41.html
- **Calvin:** notes that Christ applies the verse to Judas. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/41-9.html

**v. 1: what "considering" means.** A writer quoted in Spurgeon's Treasury notes thinks the main sense is judging the afflicted fairly and kindly, not assuming their suffering proves sin, as Job's friends did. Most commentators take it as practical help. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps041.cfm

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- NET notes: the psalmist describes himself as the person who treats the poor well. Verses 4–10 retell the prayer he prayed earlier. The meaning of "made a heel great" (v. 9) is uncertain because the phrase occurs only here. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=41
- Maclaren mentions scholars who date the psalm after the exile and read it as being about Israel as a nation. He says they have not been able to identify Israel's false friends. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/41.htm
- Maclaren also says that seeing suffering as the result of sin (v. 4) belongs to the psalmist's stage of revelation, and Christians should not hold it "in the same absolute fashion". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-41.html

**Catholic**
- Augustine's exposition on New Advent reads the psalm as the voice of Christ, sometimes speaking as the Head and sometimes as his Body, the Church. Part of it is about the mockers at the Cross. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801041.htm
  - **Check before using:** Augustine numbered the psalms differently (LXX/Vulgate), and I couldn't open the full page to confirm this is the same psalm.
- The Douay-Rheims translates v. 9 as "hath greatly supplanted me". https://biblehub.com/psalms/41-9.htm

**Promise or general rule (vv. 1–3).** The bible.org commentary warns that these lines are general wisdom statements, not promises that hold for every person every time, "We live in a fallen world!" https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-41
Matthew Henry makes a similar point under v. 3. These are useful for any discussion of health-and-wealth readings, but neither source mentions prosperity teaching by name.
